explanations.explanation: The astrologers answer in Aramaic, "O king, may you live forever! Tell your servants the dream, and we will give the interpretation." Sounds polite, right? They're asking for the one thing they need to start. It's like a mechanic saying, "Just tell me what the noise sounds like," except the noise is inside the king's head.

No deadline gets requested here. The astrologers ask the king to tell his servants the dream so they can give the interpretation. Time does come up in this story, but it's Daniel who asks for it later (Daniel 2:16). Nobody asks for a calendar yet, friend.

With the word astrologers in the room, I get why you went there. But the text has them ask for something else: "Tell your servants the dream, and we will give the interpretation." They want the dream out of the king's mouth first. Stargazing isn't part of this request.

explanations.answer: Both the dream and its interpretation
explanations.explanation: The king says, "If you do not tell me the dream and its interpretation, you will be cut into pieces and your houses will be reduced to rubble." Read that again. He wants them to say what he dreamed AND what it means. That's like your boss saying, "Write the email I'm thinking of, then answer it."

explanations.answer: Only the interpretation of his dream
explanations.explanation: That's what the wise men were hoping for. They asked the king to tell them the dream so they could give the interpretation. But the king asks for more than that. He says, "If you do not tell me the dream and its interpretation…" and that's the part that sinks them.

explanations.answer: A potion to help him sleep at night
explanations.explanation: I'd have taken that deal too, since sleep had escaped him (Daniel 2:1). But no potion comes up anywhere in this scene. The king demands that they tell him the dream and its interpretation. Nothing about a nightcap.

The king says, "I know for sure that you are stalling for time because you see that my word is final." He has heard this request twice now, and he's done. I've stalled on a few things in my day myself. A king who's already decided is the worst person to try it on.
Fair guess, since these men have a lot riding on this. But the king doesn't use that word. He says he knows for sure they are stalling for time. He sees the second request as a delay.

They did make an offer: let the king tell the dream, and they'll give the interpretation. But that's not the word the king uses. He says he knows for sure that they are stalling for time. To him it's a stall, not a deal.

The king says the opposite. He tells them, "You have conspired to speak before me false and fraudulent words, hoping the situation will change." So in his eyes they are not being honest at all. He adds that if they tell him the dream, he'll know they can give him its interpretation.

The king says, "You have conspired to speak before me false and fraudulent words, hoping the situation will change." Those are strong words. He doesn't think they're being honest, and he wants the dream told so he can know they can give him its interpretation.

The astrologers say, "What the king requests is so difficult that no one can tell it to him except the gods, whose dwelling is not with mortals." They're telling the king this is beyond any person. Keep that line in your pocket, because Daniel is about to answer it.

The text says the astrologers did name an exception. They tell the king, "…no one can tell it to him except the gods, whose dwelling is not with mortals." So they say only the gods could do it, and no one on earth. That's the claim Daniel will answer later in the story.

The decree says the wise men are to be executed, and men go looking for Daniel and his friends to execute them. Daniel is one of the king's wise men, and his friends are Hananiah, Mishael and Azariah (Daniel 2:17). The order doesn't skip anybody. I think that's a heavy moment for these four.
Ezra, a priest and scribe (Ezra 7:11), and Nehemiah, a governor of Judah (Nehemiah 5:14), are real Bible men. But they aren't in this story. The king's men come looking for Daniel and his friends.
Jeremiah was a prophet, and Baruch was his scribe (Jeremiah 36:4). They're good names, but they aren't in this scene. The men sent out by the decree go looking for Daniel and his friends.

explanations.answer: Why the king's decree is so harsh
explanations.explanation: Daniel asks, "Why is the decree from the king so harsh?" Notice the calm. A guard commander is at his door about an execution, and Daniel asks a question instead of panicking. Then Arioch explains the situation to him.

explanations.answer: Who gave the king the idea
explanations.explanation: Daniel never asks that. The text says he responds with discretion and tact, and what he asks is, "Why is the decree from the king so harsh?" He wants to understand the situation. He isn't hunting for someone to blame.

explanations.answer: When the order will be carried out
explanations.explanation: That's a very human question to ask with a guard standing there. But Daniel asks something else: "Why is the decree from the king so harsh?" He wants the reason for the decree. Then Arioch explains the situation to him.

Daniel goes in and asks the king to give him some time, so that he could give him the interpretation. The astrologers asked for the dream, but Daniel asks for time. A man walking in to ask a favor of the king who just ordered the execution takes nerve. I'd have sent a card.
Gold shows up later in this story, but not here. Daniel doesn't ask the king for money. He asks for some time, so that he could give him the interpretation.
Daniel doesn't ask for soldiers. The soldiers are the ones looking for him! What he asks the king for is some time, so that he could give him the interpretation.

Daniel urges his friends to plead for mercy from the God of heaven concerning this mystery, so that he and his friends would not be killed with the rest of the wise men of Babylon. Four men, one prayer request. When the problem is bigger than you, you go to the One who isn't.
Rain would be a fine thing to ask for in some other story. Here the friends are urged to plead for mercy from the God of heaven concerning this mystery. Their lives depend on it.

Nobody's going to war in this scene. Daniel urges his friends to plead for mercy from the God of heaven concerning this mystery. The goal is that they would not be killed with the rest of the wise men of Babylon.

explanations.answer: He blesses the God of heaven
explanations.explanation: The text says that during the night, the mystery was revealed to Daniel in a vision, and he blessed the God of heaven. The first thing out of his mouth is praise, not a victory lap. Then he declares the praise out loud, and we get to hear it in the next verses.

explanations.answer: He goes right back to sleep
explanations.explanation: After a day like that, I'd want a nap too. But the text doesn't have Daniel rolling over. It says the mystery was revealed to him in a vision, and he blessed the God of heaven.

explanations.answer: He writes it down on a scroll
explanations.explanation: That would be a smart move, but it's not in the text. Daniel blesses the God of heaven and then declares his praise. No scroll, no note, just worship.

Daniel says of God, "He changes the times and seasons; He removes kings and establishes them." Hold on to that. He's saying it about a king who can order the whole wise-men crew executed, and Daniel says the God of heaven is the One who sets kings up.

It's in his praise, word for word: "He changes the times and seasons; He removes kings and establishes them." Daniel says this to God, with a king's decree hanging over his head. He knows who is really in charge.

Daniel says the opposite: "He reveals the deep and hidden things; He knows what lies in darkness, and light dwells with Him." Nothing is hidden from God. The king's dream was locked away from every wise man in Babylon, and God knew it all along.

Daniel says, "He reveals the deep and hidden things; He knows what lies in darkness, and light dwells with Him." God does know what lies in darkness. That's exactly why He could reveal a dream that nobody in the room could touch.

Daniel tells Arioch, "Do not execute the wise men of Babylon! Bring me before the king, and I will give him the interpretation." Arioch is the man the king appointed to destroy them, so this is a big ask. Daniel isn't just saving himself here. He's speaking up for the whole group.
The king summoned the wise men at the start (Daniel 2:2), so I see how that stuck. But Daniel's request is bigger: "Do not execute the wise men of Babylon!" He asks to be brought before the king.
Questioning is what Daniel did earlier when he asked Arioch why the decree was so harsh. This time he says, "Do not execute the wise men of Babylon!" That's a much bolder line.

explanations.answer: None of them can explain this mystery
explanations.explanation: Daniel says, "No wise man, enchanter, medium, or magician can explain to the king the mystery of which he inquires." The wise men themselves said as much (Daniel 2:10). Daniel doesn't take the credit. He's about to point somewhere else.

explanations.answer: They knew the dream all along
explanations.explanation: If they did, this chapter would be a lot shorter. The astrologers told the king that no one on earth could do what he asked (Daniel 2:10). Daniel agrees that none of them can explain this mystery.

explanations.answer: They should be put in charge of it
explanations.explanation: Daniel goes the other way. He says, "No wise man, enchanter, medium, or magician can explain to the king the mystery of which he inquires." Nobody on that list is getting the job.

explanations.answer: What will happen in the future
explanations.explanation: Daniel says God "has made known to King Nebuchadnezzar what will happen in the latter days." He calls God "the Revealer of Mysteries" in the next verse. The king lay on his bed thinking about the future, and God showed him what's ahead.

explanations.answer: Which of his officials lied to him
explanations.explanation: The king did accuse the wise men of speaking false and fraudulent words (Daniel 2:9). But that's not what Daniel says the dream is about. He says God has made known to the king what will happen in the latter days.
That would be a different kind of dream. Daniel says God "has made known to King Nebuchadnezzar what will happen in the latter days." It looks ahead.

Daniel says the opposite: "…not because I have more wisdom than any man alive, but in order that the interpretation might be made known to the king…" He's handing the credit away before anyone offers it. I know what it's like to be handed something I didn't earn. I got pulled out of a junk drawer, friend.

Daniel says the mystery was revealed "…not because I have more wisdom than any man alive, but in order that the interpretation might be made known to the king, and that you may understand the thoughts of your mind." Daniel keeps the spotlight off himself. It's a humble thing to say to a king.

Daniel says its legs were iron, and "its feet were part iron and part clay." Strong metal on top, and something that crumbles at the very bottom. Remember that, because the stone goes right for those feet.
Bronze is up higher. The statue's belly and thighs were bronze, and its legs were iron. The feet were part iron and part clay.
The gold is at the very top, since the head of the statue was pure gold. The stone isn't part of the statue. It's cut out later, and it hits the statue. The feet were part iron and part clay.

Daniel says the stone "struck the statue on its feet of iron and clay, and crushed them." It goes right for the weak spot. A cookie jar on a high shelf has the same problem, but I'm not saying this is that.
The stone did hit the feet. Daniel says it "struck the statue on its feet of iron and clay, and crushed them." The stone was cut out, but not by human hands.

Daniel says, "…the stone that had struck the statue became a great mountain and filled the whole earth." A small stone that ends up filling the whole earth. The statue got shattered and blown away, and the stone grew.
No fire in this dream. The pieces of the statue are carried off by the wind, and the stone becomes something else. Daniel says it became a great mountain and filled the whole earth.
A river would spread out nicely, but that's not what happens. The stone that struck the statue became a great mountain. And it filled the whole earth.
Daniel tells the king, "You are that head of gold." The king gets the top spot and the best metal. I'd have taken that spot too, no question.
Silver is the next kingdom, and Daniel says it comes after Nebuchadnezzar. The king himself is the part at the top. Daniel says, "You are that head of gold."
The iron legs come much later in the line. Daniel says the fourth kingdom is as strong as iron. Nebuchadnezzar is the head: "You are that head of gold."

Daniel says, "…for iron shatters and crushes all things, and like iron that crushes all things, it will shatter and crush all the others." That's a kingdom with no gentle side. The picture is iron doing what iron does.
Not with this one. Daniel says the fourth kingdom is as strong as iron, and "it will shatter and crush all the others." Iron isn't known for negotiating.
It's the other direction. Daniel says this kingdom "will shatter and crush all the others." Iron doesn't take orders from bronze.
Daniel says the opposite. He says, "…so this will be a divided kingdom, yet some of the strength of iron will be in it." It's a mix that doesn't blend. He calls it partly strong and partly brittle.

Daniel calls it "a divided kingdom, yet some of the strength of iron will be in it—just as you saw the iron mixed with clay." So it has strength, but it's split. The peoples will mix with one another but will not hold together.
Daniel says the kingdom God sets up "will never be destroyed, nor will it be left to another people." So it doesn't change hands. Every kingdom in the statue gets replaced, but this one doesn't.

Daniel says the God of heaven will set up a kingdom "that will never be destroyed, nor will it be left to another people." It's the one kingdom in this whole story that never gets passed along. It "will itself stand forever."

The text says King Nebuchadnezzar "fell on his face, paid homage to Daniel." This is the king who ordered the execution of the wise men. Now he's on the floor. I think that's a moment he did not see coming that morning.
That could have happened in a different chapter. Here the king fell on his face, paid homage to Daniel, and ordered that an offering and incense be presented to him. Then he promoted Daniel.
He doesn't call them back. The wise men had already said no one could do this, and Daniel's God was the One who showed it. The king fell on his face and paid homage to Daniel.

The king says, "Your God is truly the God of gods and Lord of kings, the Revealer of Mysteries, since you were able to reveal this mystery." A king says that about somebody else's God. Big words from a man who'd been so angry hours earlier.
He does say it. The king tells Daniel, "Your God is truly the God of gods and Lord of kings, the Revealer of Mysteries, since you were able to reveal this mystery." That's the king, out loud.

The king made Daniel "ruler over the entire province of Babylon and chief administrator over all the wise men of Babylon." That's a long way from standing outside waiting on a guard commander. Daniel ends the chapter with a big job.
Judah is Daniel's homeland, and Arioch called him one of "the exiles from Judah" (Daniel 2:25). But the king doesn't put him over Judah. He makes Daniel ruler over the entire province of Babylon.
Persia doesn't come up in this chapter. The king is in Babylon, and that's where Daniel is promoted. He becomes ruler over the entire province of Babylon.

The king made Daniel "ruler over the entire province of Babylon and chief administrator over all the wise men of Babylon." That's the same group that was almost executed. Daniel went from being counted among them to being in charge of them.

It's right there in verse 48: the king "made him ruler over the entire province of Babylon and chief administrator over all the wise men of Babylon." He got two jobs, and the second one is over the wise men.
At Daniel's request, the king appointed Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego to manage the province of Babylon. Those are the three friends he asked to pray with him. Daniel remained in the king's court.
Arioch, the commander of the king's guard, is part of this story. But the king doesn't name him here. At Daniel's request, the king appointed Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego.
Ashpenaz was chief of the king's court officials (Daniel 1:3). He's not in this scene. The king appoints Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, at Daniel's request.
